reader.title: Killing of Simon Woods
bases: A deputy sheriff serving a warrant shot and killed Woods while, by the officer-side accounts, Woods resisted arrest with a gun; no crowd or mob took part (A5, A6, A7).

Two separate Opelousas weeklies with differing details (A5, A6) and an Opelousas dispatch (A7, A1) agree that Deputy McKinney shot and killed Woods while arresting him, though every account gives the officer's side.

summary.text: The killing of Simon Woods was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff E. A. McKinney at Wilson's sawmill on Bayou Cocodrie, near Opelousas, Louisiana, on the evening of 16 May 1882.
McKinney said he fired when Woods reached for a shotgun as he was being arrested, and a coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide.
A New Orleans Picayune wire carried the news as far as Texas, Virginia, Georgia and Tennessee under headlines calling Woods a horse thief.
Woods was charged in St. Landry Parish with horse stealing and assault and battery, according to the Opelousas Courier and an Opelousas dispatch.
Both papers also described him as a fugitive from St. Martin Parish, where he was said to face a charge of stabbing a man.

The St. Landry Democrat gave a different cause for the warrant: Anderson Stewart, a Black man living at the mill, swore an affidavit after Woods allegedly took his thirteen-year-old daughter, tried to cut his wife's throat with a knife, and threatened to kill him.
Mill owner Wilson warned the deputy that Woods carried a double-barreled shotgun and had threatened to kill anyone who tried to arrest him.
To avoid alarming Woods, McKinney traded clothes with a mill hand, who rode off on the deputy's horse, and took the man's place at work with a borrowed shotgun.
Late in the evening Woods came to the mill office, set down his gun and, by the Democrat's account, told those present he wanted his quarrel with Stewart settled.

When McKinney announced that Woods was his prisoner, Woods took up his gun; the Democrat said McKinney fired as Woods jerked it up, while the Courier said Woods had cocked both barrels and was raising it to his shoulder.
The charge struck Woods in the side or bowels, and he died before or on the next morning.
According to the Courier and the Opelousas dispatch, Woods said before dying that the officer had been right to shoot him because he had resolved not to be taken.
The Democrat reported that the coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, and no report of further proceedings appears in the coverage.
Every surviving account told the story from the officer's side, and none recorded a version from Woods's family or other Black witnesses.

The local weeklies called Woods a "colored desperado" and a "dangerous and desperate character," and the Lake Charles Commercial headlined its item "A Desperate Negro Killed by an Officer While Resisting Arrest," calling him "the terror of the neighborhood."

Beyond Louisiana, the two-sentence Picayune wire ran on 18 and 19 May in the Dallas Daily Herald, the Richmond Daily Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, closing with the line that McKinney "saved his own life by being an expert shot."
Headlines such as "Horse Thief Shot" and "A Horse-Thief Killed" presented the accusation as fact and did not mention Woods's race.
The papers disagreed on where the mill stood, the Courier placing it about twenty-four miles northwest of Opelousas and the dispatch about twelve miles northeast.
They also differed on the charge, with the Courier and the wire citing horse stealing and assault and battery and the Democrat describing Stewart's affidavit over the attack on his wife.

accounts.label: St. Landry Democrat (local, officer's side)
accounts.gist: After Stewart's affidavit, McKinney lured Woods to the mill office by disguise; Woods seized his gun when told he was a prisoner and McKinney fired as Woods jerked it up; both barrels were found cocked.

accounts.label: Opelousas Courier (local, officer's side)
accounts.gist: Woods, charged with horse stealing and assault and battery, picked up his gun, cocked both barrels and began raising it, and McKinney fired 'just in time to save his own life'; Woods said before dying that the officer had done right.

accounts.label: Opelousas dispatch / Picayune wire
accounts.gist: Woods leveled a double-barrel gun and McKinney shot first; the short wire said McKinney 'saved his own life by being an expert shot.'

framing.detail: Local papers called Woods a 'colored desperado' and 'dangerous and desperate character' and said McKinney fired to save his life.
The Lake Charles headline read 'A Desperate Negro Killed by an Officer While Resisting Arrest' and called Woods 'the terror of the neighborhood.'
Out-of-state dailies ran the two-sentence Picayune wire under headlines such as 'Horse Thief Shot' and 'A Horse-Thief Killed.'
